edits.walkthrough_append: Board takeaway: expect one theory question on why Bohr's orbits are called stationary states, and a one-marker on what hydrogen spectrum lines represent — electron jumps between fixed energy levels. Self-check: explain in two lines why an electron in the first shell does not spiral into the nucleus even though opposite charges attract. If you can connect quantised energy levels to the line spectrum, the question is yours; examiners award the mark for the phrase 'specific energy difference', not for naming colours.

Board takeaway: questions usually give a table of fish catch or a map and ask you to relate it to ocean conditions — practise naming the zone (coastal waters, EEZ, deep sea) and one reason for richness (upwelling brings nutrients to the surface). Self-check: state in one sentence the difference between the territorial sea and the EEZ, and which one India alone may fish in. Answers that name both the legal zone and the physical process score full marks.

Board takeaway: the classic proof runs — given l parallel to m and m parallel to n, suppose l met n at some point P; then two different parallels to m would pass through P, which the parallel postulate forbids — so l is parallel to n. Write the contradiction explicitly; examiners award the method mark for it. Self-check: fill in the blank — lines that are parallel to the same line are ____ to each other — and justify with the postulate in one sentence.

Board takeaway: expect a two-marker on why a point and a line are left undefined in Euclid's geometry, and a one-marker asking which definition or postulate a given statement uses. Answer with the circularity argument: every definition needs simpler terms, and the chain must stop somewhere. Self-check: write down two physical objects that model a plane poorly and say why — a sheet of paper, for instance, has edges and thickness, while a Euclidean plane has neither.

Board takeaway: a four-marker often asks how Indian culture reached Southeast Asia — structure the answer as traders and monks first, Sanskrit texts and temple styles second, local rulers adopting them to raise their prestige third. Self-check: give one example of an Indianised monument outside India (Borobudur or Angkor Wat) and name the religion it reflects. Stress the word 'voluntary' — the adoption-by-local-rulers point is what separates a strong answer from a conquest narrative.

Board takeaway: write SAS in full — two sides and the angle included between them — and mark the given parts on a rough figure before proving; the figure earns the presentation mark. Self-check: for the carpenter's shelves, state why the 60° angle must sit between the 30 cm and 40 cm sides for SAS to apply, and what could go wrong if it lay elsewhere. If the angle is not included, the data no longer fixes the third side uniquely.

Board takeaway: a common three-marker asks why a fractionating column is needed for close boiling points — answer in steps: vapours of both liquids rise, repeated condensation and revaporisation on the glass beads enrich the vapour in the more volatile liquid, and the pure component condenses in the condenser. Self-check: name the part that provides surface for the repeated cycles, and state which liquid distils first when acetone (56°C) and methanol (65°C) are separated. Quoting the boiling points earns credit.

Board takeaway: finish the tank problem completely — V = (4/3) × (22/7) × 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5, about 14.14 cubic metres, then multiply by 1000 to report roughly 14,140 litres; the conversion step carries its own mark, so never stop at cubic metres. Self-check: recompute with the radius doubled — the volume becomes 8 times larger, because volume scales as the cube of the radius. This scaling idea is a favourite one-marker.

Board takeaway: learn the model's three claims — a positive sphere, electrons embedded in it, overall neutrality — and one limitation each for Thomson and for Rutherford; comparison questions are frequent. Self-check: sketch the plum pudding, label where the electrons sit, then write one line on why the model cannot explain the alpha-scattering observations. Naming the 1897 cathode ray studies and the particle discovered earns the first mark in most answers.

Board takeaway: state the axiom in full — if a ray stands on a line, the sum of the two adjacent angles so formed is 180° — and quote it by name whenever a proof uses it. Self-check: one angle of a linear pair is three times the other; set up x + 3x = 180° and get 45° and 135°. Numerical drills like this appear as two-markers; always write the equation line before solving.

Board takeaway: keep the diagnostic chain ready — diagonals bisect each other (parallelogram), are equal (rectangle), are perpendicular (rhombus), both at once (square). Objective questions hand you one diagonal property and ask for the shape. Self-check: a window frame has equal diagonals that are not perpendicular; classify it and justify in one line. Answer in the order condition-then-shape: 'rectangle, because the diagonals are equal' earns both marks, the bare word only one.

Board takeaway: compute sodium chloride's formula unit mass once cleanly — 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u — and reuse the pattern for calcium carbonate (100 u) and magnesium chloride (95 u). Say 'formula unit mass', never 'molecular mass', for ionic compounds; the terminology itself carries a mark. Self-check: add 24 + 2 × 35.5 and confirm 95 u for MgCl₂. Show the atomic masses you picked from the table; hidden working loses the method mark even when the answer is right.

Board takeaway: property answers score through reasons, not adjectives — write 'ions are locked in the lattice and cannot move, so the solid does not conduct', not just 'ionic compounds do not conduct'. Self-check: explain in one sentence why solid sodium chloride does not conduct but molten sodium chloride does, and why wax melts on a warm spoon while salt does not. Three contrast rows — melting point, conductivity, solubility — each with its structural reason, is the full-credit format.

Board takeaway: Riya's second strip must meet the wall at 55°, because 35° + 55° = 90°; write the sum equation before substituting, since the equation line carries the method mark. Self-check: the supplement of 105° is 75°, but its complement does not exist, because no angle above 90° has a complement. Papers test exactly this boundary — always check whether the given angle exceeds the benchmark before answering.

Board takeaway: present the proof as a two-step chain — alternate interior angles equal, then the linear pair — citing the earlier result by name at each step; examiners mark the citations. Self-check: co-interior angles between parallel lines are in the ratio 2 : 3; set 2x + 3x = 180° to get 72° and 108°. Numerical use of supplementary co-interior angles is a reliable two-marker; always state in words which angle pair you are using.

Board takeaway: reproduce the diagonal proof in three lines — alternate angles from the two pairs of parallel sides, the common side AC, then CPCT — and the properties follow in one sentence. Self-check: in a parallelogram ABCD with angle A = 70°, find the other three angles (C = 70°, B = D = 110°). The opposite-sides-equal facts are one-markers; the diagonal proof is the three-marker — memorise the citation order, not a paragraph.

Board takeaway: in chromatography answers, label the diagram with stationary phase (paper), mobile phase (solvent) and the separated spots; a labelled diagram carries the mark even when the written explanation falters. Self-check: predict which of two dyes travels farther if it dissolves better in the solvent, and justify with the adsorption-versus-solubility balance in one line. Keep two applications ready — separating ink or dyes, and drug tests in forensics — for the one-markers.

Board takeaway: state the law verbatim — matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — because the statement itself carries a mark. Self-check: in 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂, verify with atomic masses (Hg = 201, O = 16) that 434 mass units of red powder yield exactly 402 + 32 mass units of products. Mention the closed container when explaining why the balance stayed constant — escaping gas is the classic trap the sealed jar prevents.

Board takeaway: name the condition completely — right angle, hypotenuse, one other side — and mark the right angle with a small square in the figure; omitting the hypotenuse label is the commonest presentation slip. Self-check: with hypotenuse 13 cm and one side 5 cm, the third side is 12 cm by Pythagoras, and any two such 5-12-13 triangles are congruent by RHS. Examiners often pair a Pythagoras computation with an RHS proof; keep the steps in that order.

Board takeaway: structure a UPI answer as actors and flow — the app, the NPCI switch, the sender's bank, the receiver's bank — and note that the VPA hides account details, which is exactly the security point examiners want. Self-check: list one safeguard the MPIN provides and one the QR code provides, and name the organisation that operates the switch. One-marker favourites: what UPI stands for, the role of NPCI, and what a VPA is.

Board takeaway: compare the three mixture types in a table — particle size, stability, filterability, Tyndall effect — because the comparison format is the standard four-marker. Self-check: state why muddy flood water is a suspension and what becomes of it in a reservoir; the phrase 'settle under gravity' must appear. Fix the thresholds: about 1 nm for true solutions, above 1000 nm for suspensions, colloids in between — quoting both numbers earns both marks.

Board takeaway: show the criss-cross visibly in your working — symbols, valencies, then the crossed-over subscripts — because the method mark lives in the intermediate step, not the final formula. Self-check: write the formulae for aluminium oxide and ammonium sulphate; they are Al₂O₃ and (NH₄)₂SO₄. Watch the two traps: simplify the ratio when both valencies share a factor, and put a polyatomic ion in brackets before subscripting it. Practise until the four-step routine takes under a minute.

Board takeaway: the extend-DE-to-F construction with the doubled segment is the examiner's favourite proof; practise writing it in five named steps — construction, congruence by ASA, CPCT, parallelogram identification, conclusion. Self-check: in triangle ABC, D and E are the midpoints of AB and AC with BC = 8 cm; state DE immediately as 4 cm, parallel to BC. Numerical one-markers ask exactly this, while the full proof is the three-marker — both spring from the same theorem.

Board takeaway: a five-marker on Mughal administration should name and define each term — mansabdar, zat, sawar, jagir, zabt — then close with one sentence on why this salaried bureaucracy outperformed the Sultanate's hereditary nobles. Self-check: explain in two lines how jagirs linked land revenue to troop maintenance, and what went wrong when jagirdars demanded more than the peasants could pay. Definitions plus the revenue-salary link is the scoring combination.

Board takeaway: compute Riya's four walls as 2 × 3 × (5 + 4) = 54 square metres, then reason about paint coverage — this two-stage habit matches how application questions are marked. Self-check: subtract the doors and windows whenever the question lists them; that twist appears in at least one variant every year. Keep the decision line handy — 'walls only' or 'open box' means lateral surface area, 'closed box' means total — and write it before substituting numbers.

Board takeaway: the proof skeleton is — draw a diagonal, prove the two triangles congruent by SSS, transfer angles by CPCT, and conclude both pairs of opposite sides are parallel; write these four headings before filling in details. Self-check: with the door frame's 210 cm and 90 cm pieces, the diagonal completes two triangles whose three sides all match — that is why SSS applies. Quote CPCT explicitly; jumping straight to parallelism drops the reasoning mark.

Board takeaway: electron-dot structures must show every valence electron, including the lone pairs; examiners deduct for missing dots even when the bonding pair is correct. Self-check: draw O₂ — two shared pairs form the double bond and each oxygen keeps two lone pairs — then count eight electrons around each atom to confirm the octet. Keep the ladder ready: one shared pair is a single bond (chlorine), two a double bond (oxygen), three a triple bond (nitrogen).

Board takeaway: split any 'exactly one' proof into the two halves examiners mark separately — construct the parallel line (existence), then assume a second one and derive a contradiction (uniqueness). Self-check: state what goes wrong if two distinct lines through the same point were both parallel to the given line — the angle sums contradict the parallel postulate. This two-part structure returns when you prove the angle sum property of a triangle, so master it once here.

Board takeaway: the classification table — solution, colloid, suspension against particle size, stability, filterability and Tyndall effect — is the highest-yield revision page of this chapter; reproduce it from memory twice before the exam. Self-check: classify fog, muddy river water and vinegar, and justify each with one observable property. Boundary lines earn marks: colloids show the Tyndall effect but never settle, suspensions always settle, and true solutions do neither.
